newsitem.title: USA: US FCC officials race to resolve digital TV rules.
newsitem.headline: US FCC officials race to resolve digital TV rules.

text.p: Officials from the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday raced to resolve how quickly television stations should roll out high-definition digital broadcasts to consumers over the next 2-1/2 years.

Officials were hopeful they could resolve the issue in time for an FCC public meeting Thursday when the agency's four commissioners would have the chance to approve overall rules for doling out digital TV licenses, officials said.
If that deadline is not met, the agency still could approve the rules by week's end.
"I remain optimistic that the commission can resolve all open issues today and adopt our final two digital television orders tomorrow," Commissioner Susan Ness said in a statement Wednesday.
Ness, a key player in talks over the digital roll-out, said the timetable should be "aggressive but not precipitous."
The commisioner has sought voluntary commitments from network-affiliated stations in the top 10 metropolitan areas for an 18-month timetable.

"At least two dozen stations have stepped up to this challenge," Ness said. "I am comfortable relying on these commitments, backstopped by a 24-month rule for network affiliates in the top 10 markets and a 30-month rule for all network affiliates in the top 30 markets."
Souces said that while three of the agency's commissioners can support such an approach, FCC Chairman Reed Hundt has been pushing for a more aggressive timetable.
"We're hoping he'll recognize that what we've got is good enough," said one official who requested anonymity.

To jump-start the digital age, Hundt wants to ensure that a substantial number of households can receive the broadcasts so TV manufacturers have enough incentive to ship digital sets in time for the important Christmas shopping season in 1998.

"I believe that the voluntary commitment of major broadcasters to be on air in the top 10 markets in time for the 1998 Christmas season, coupled with the commitment of television manufacturers to have sets in the hands of consumers in those markets on that schedule, will fuel the rapid rollout of digital television," said Ness.
Meanwhile, the decision by Congress not to require TV stations to pay for use of the digital airwaves drew further criticism from consumer advocates and others.
"What they're getting for free is public property, as much as our national parks are public property," Donald Case, vice president of Common Cause, said of the decision.
FCC estimates suggest an auction of the digital licenses could fetch as much as $70 billion, prompting critics to say TV stations are getting a multi-billion dollar "giveaway."
Case said a report issued Wednesday by the consumer lobbying group showed broadcasters had "mastered the Washington-influence money game."
The report said the top 10 broadcast interests, along with the National Association of Broadcasters, gave $9.5 million in political contributions during the past decade.
NAB spokesman Dennis Wharton said any suggestion that broadcasters had bought off Congress were "so baseless they barely merit a response."

He also rejected the suggestion that broadcasters are the recipients of a giveaway. "This is not a giveaway. This is a loan to ensure a smooth transition for consumers from analog to digital television," said Wharton.
"At the end of the transition, broadcasters will be operating with one third less spectrum than they use currently. That is a giveback, not a giveaway."

An FCC official later said that negotiators at the agency had agreed on an immediate recovery of channels 60-69 from TV broadcasters. Twenty-four Megahertz (MHz) of that spectrum would be allocated for use by public safety officials around the country while 36 MHz would be auctioned by the government for other uses.

The officials also agreed that TV stations, once they received their digital licenses, would not be required to provide high-definition broadcasts. That way stations could provide up to five channels of lower definition broadcasts via their digital channels. Officials continued to negotiate over what type of public interest obligations to impose on stations in the new digital age.
